chunks: "EMI, electromagnetic interference, is unwanted electromagnetic energy that disturbs the operation of a circuit or system.
It always has three parts: a source that makes it, a coupling path, and a victim that's affected.
The same word covers energy the board emits, which can interfere with radios and fail compliance, and energy that arrives from outside and upsets the board, which is an immunity question.
There are two ways it travels. Conducted EMI moves along wires, power lines and shared grounds. Radiated EMI moves through the air as fields.
On a PCB, nearly all the radiated EMI comes from two things: current loops, which act as small magnetic antennas, and common-mode current on cables, which acts as a short monopole.
The big point is that EMI comes from edges and currents, not just clock frequency.
A trapezoidal digital signal has harmonics out to about one over pi times the rise time, so a 10 megahertz clock with a 2 nanosecond edge still has meaningful content at 150 megahertz and beyond.
That's why slowing the edge, shrinking the loop and controlling the return path are the usual first fixes, and why EMC testing runs up to a gigahertz and beyond."
